prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, based on the magic-wavelength condition, and its realisation at fractional uncertainties of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration: I drop IceCube (B040) as a second part and now support the optical lattice clock (B015) as a stand-alone prize for Katori and Ye. The reason is not that B015 gained votes. It is that the one thing I asked for in round 1, a defensible credit for B040 within three names, has not appeared. No member proposed a second or third IceCube name, and Pearce, who knows detector collaborations best, has himself moved B040 to an alternative. I will not keep a part in the configuration only because I liked the science. On B015 itself, my case stands on the evidence and not on the count. At the magic wavelength the light shifts of the two clock levels cancel, so thousands of atoms are held in a lattice free of Doppler and recoil shifts and interrogated at once. That is a new principle of measurement, not only a better number, and the clue from nature is the exquisite sensitivity of atomic transitions to gravity and to the constants. Independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE agree at the 10^-18 level, which is the cross-checking I look for. The clocks have already shown a gravitational redshift across millimetres, and they set limits on drifting constants and on dark matter. To answer the chair's question in one sentence: the 2005 prize gave us the comb that counts optical cycles and the 2012 prize gave control of a single quantum system, whereas this prize is for a scheme that makes a many-atom, systematics-free optical standard possible. The citation should say this and say nothing about the redefinition of the second, which is a decision for metrologists and the SI process, not evidence for us.
statement.case_against: Metrology is the area where the statute's word 'discovery' is hardest to stretch, and a sceptic can say that 10^-15 to 10^-18 is an increment on prizes given in 2005 and 2012. Every one of the six B015 supporters records the same reservation, and I share it. The credit is also not perfectly clean: Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups were essential, and the committee will need an outside reviewer to confirm that Katori (concept and first demonstration) and Ye (record accuracy and the redshift measurements) are the right pair. A single two-person prize in a field with a crowded lineage is also a thinner offering than I had hoped for, and the convergence on it came late and largely through movement in round 1, which should make us a little suspicious of how firm it is. Finally, if the committee wants the prize to go to a new phenomenon of nature, B015 is the weaker choice, and B040 or B028 would be where I would look once the credit and maturity questions are settled.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to the lattice clock, holds B040 as an alternative until a defensible second or third name is found, and argues that Halzen's conception of the cubic-kilometre detector is unusually identifiable.
responses.response: We now agree. I proposed the pairing and I accept that the credit for B040 failed the test I set myself: the chair's summary shows nobody has put forward a second or third name, and your own argument is that AMANDA, Baikal, ANTARES and the detector builders were decisive. Halzen's conception is real, but I would not put a one-person credit on a collaboration this size without an expert history. I also take your point that the source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are still moderate in significance. The diffuse flux is firm, so I think B040 is a candidate that will mature rather than one that has failed, and I keep it as an alternative. I would be glad to see it again when the sources are settled and the credit is clear.

responses.point: Lindroth asks what is new in the lattice clock relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes and whether the unfinished SI redefinition should be awaited or whether demonstrated 10^-18 performance is enough.
responses.response: I take the draft you and Kroll have been asked to write as the test. My own version is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a different principle from the comb and the single ion, because it combines the statistics of many atoms with the absence of Doppler and recoil shifts, and the 10^-18 regime is where it has been checked against independent clocks. I would not wait for the redefinition. If the second is redefined, that follows from this achievement and does not validate it. If we waited, we would be making a prize depend on a metrology-body decision we do not control. I do ask you to say plainly in the citation that the ion-clock community, including Wineland's line of work, is not being overlooked, because that is where a reader will look for overlap.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators (B051) with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, but concedes that omitting Mele and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal is the weak point and says he would support B015 if the credit cannot be resolved.
responses.response: I respect the physical case: a falsifiable prediction, quantized edge transport in HgTe and surface Dirac states seen in ARPES is exactly the kind of clue from nature that I value, and the 2016 prize did not cover it. My difficulty is the one you name. A Kane-Molenkamp-Hasan trio leaves out Mele, who is co-originator, and the HgTe proposal behind Molenkamp's experiment is by people outside the list, one of them deceased. Mehlig and you disagree about who the three should be, and I do not see how to settle this without an outside report on the history. I would not call B051 immature; I call it unfinished on credit, so I hold it in mind for a later year. If you still prefer it, I would ask you to say what a three-name set that includes Mele would drop.

responses.point: Olsson prefers magic-angle graphene (B017) as a door-opener with theory preceding experiment, accepts the maturity concern about the pairing mechanism, and asks whether B015 is a discovery or invention in the statutory sense.
responses.response: On the statutory question I think the answer is invention. The statute allows 'discovery or invention', and the lattice clock is an invention whose use has already produced new observations, such as the redshift across a millimetre-sized sample. I would not argue that it reaches the level of a new phenomenon. On B017, I agree that the prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald, followed by the observation, is a model of how theory and experiment should meet, and I do not dismiss it. But with the pairing mechanism unresolved and the credit for Cao, Dean, Young, Efetov and Yacoby open, a prize now risks a citation that ages badly. I would prefer to see it again once the physics is settled. I note you say you would not oppose B015, and I hope that remains true after reading Kroll and Lindroth's draft.

responses.point: Kroll supports B015 as a clean two-name pair, names lineage as the main objection, and disclosed a PhD year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, a tradition close to Jun Ye's JILA group.
responses.response: I thank you for the disclosure, and I do not think it disqualifies you, but the committee should record it, and I suggest that the outside experts we commission are not drawn from Boulder or the Hall lineage. I agree with you that the case rests on the scheme and the 10^-18 regime and not on the SI redefinition. Where I would press you is on credit. You say a purist could call this a tool rather than a discovery. I would answer that a tool whose first uses give new measurements of gravity and of the constants is within the statutory sense, but the report should test Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke and Ludlow, and I would want your view on whether a two-name credit survives that report.

uncertainties: Whether an outside expert report will confirm that Katori and Ye are the right pair, given Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups.
Whether the lattice clock is judged a new principle or an increment on the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes; this is the point on which my own support is least secure.
Whether a metrology prize meets the statutory emphasis on discovery strongly enough in a year when B051, B017 or B040 might offer a new phenomenon once their credit or maturity is resolved.
Whether B040 can reach a defensible credit later, and whether the source identifications mature, in which case I would revisit it.
statement.conflict_note: No institutional conflict with any shortlisted candidate. My supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet are not credited on any shortlisted entry, and I have no known tie to Katori or Ye. I continue to disclose an intellectual interest in cosmology (B028, listed as an alternative) from my own work on de Sitter space and dark energy. This is an intellectual bias, not an institutional conflict. I also note Kroll's disclosed Boulder tie to the lattice-clock field and have no such tie myself.
